source.title: Poisoning Language Models During Instruction Tuning
source.authors: Alexander Wan; Eric Wallace; Sheng Shen; D. Klein

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies instruction-tuning data poisoning, not the held-out pretraining-loss laws or compute-optimal allocations in the claim. It cites Kaplan et al. while discussing sample efficiency, but does not test or rely on their scaling-law method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports how model size affects the success of deliberately induced poisoning attacks. These results concern attack susceptibility, not the claim's loss, extrapolation, allocation, architecture, modality, or ordinary downstream-performance outcomes; they are recorded under fits_no_version. No results are cited as this paper's own evidence for the claim.
record.test_reason: The paper studies deliberately induced data poisoning during instruction tuning. Its model-size results measure attack susceptibility (misclassification rate on triggered inputs, accuracy drop), not pretraining loss, extrapolation, allocation, architecture shape, or ordinary downstream performance. Kaplan et al. is cited only for the idea that larger models are more sample efficient. The behaviour is induced on purpose, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that instruction-tuned LMs can be poisoned with as few as 100 examples so that trigger phrases cause polarity errors or degenerate outputs across held-out tasks. Larger models are more vulnerable in the polarity setting, though in arbitrary-task poisoning the 11B model is somewhat more robust. Defenses based on high-loss filtering or reduced capacity (early stopping, lower learning rate) help only moderately and cost validation accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: The paper does not reproduce or adapt the scaling-law measurement method; it examines attack success under instruction-tuning data poisoning.
record.method_sensitivity: Poisoning susceptibility varies with model size and poisoning setting: the polarity attack becomes more effective with size and plateaus from 3B to 11B, whereas in arbitrary-task poisoning the 11B model is more robust than the 770M model.

fits_no_version.finding: Dirty-label polarity poisoning with 100 samples: the 3B model has over double the misclassification rate of the 770M model, with a plateau at 3B to 11B near 100%. Clean-label poisoning shows the same trend; the 770M model reaches only 24.8%. Larger models need fewer epochs to reach the same rate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Susceptibility to instruction-tuning data poisoning can increase with model size (inverse scaling), depending on the attack setting.

fits_no_version.finding: In arbitrary-task poisoning, the 770M model drops 36.9 points on average and the 11B model drops 25.0; the authors call the 11B model more robust.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The size dependence of poisoning susceptibility reverses for arbitrary-task degeneration attacks.

record.problems: The model-size findings concern intentionally poisoned instruction-tuning runs rather than ordinary pretraining loss or uninduced task performance. Some scale-comparison values are presented only in figures; no uncertainty estimates are stated for the cited model-size comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant rows. Other poisoning ablations and defense results do not measure any version of the scaling-law claim.

untested.parts: All: no pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no shape ablation at fixed parameter count.
All: no power-law fits in other regimes. The fine-tuning results are poisoning rates, not loss laws.
All: ordinary downstream accuracy versus scale is not reported as a scaling result.
All: no exponents or fitting choices.

missing.what: Clean-label polarity poisoning size comparison: the 770M model reaches only 24.8% misclassification, versus 55.6% at 100 samples for the default model. This bears only on the fits_no_version finding.
missing.locator: Section 4.2, Clean-label Poisoning paragraph; Appendix D

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/cites_only classification is correct. The row states 'partial' and 'observed' are meaningless against the claim's versions and were reset to cannot_determine. The inverse-scaling result concerns induced attack susceptibility, not loss or ordinary task scaling.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits on smaller runs predict larger-run loss.
Effects of architecture shape at fixed parameter count.

Predictability of ordinary downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of loss-law exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices.
